segments.title: Why you are here and what this is

cues.text: You may know the pattern. A setup from a video looked clean on the replay, so you traded it.
Some days it worked and some days it did not. A month later you could not say whether it was the setup, the market, or you.
Nothing was written down. Not the rule, not the stop, which is the order that closes the trade when you are wrong, and not the reason for the exit.
Without a written rule and a record, every result is a story, and you cannot improve a story. A story gets better every time you tell it. A trade does not.
Now, what this is. The Blueprint is a trading framework, written down so you can build your own, with its examples on MNQ, the Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures contract.
It has six parts. One: levels, the prices where structure already happened.
Two: reads, how you judge what price is doing at a level. A level and a read together make a setup.
Three: triggers, the event that tells you to act.
Four: construction, where the stop, the size and the entry go.
Five: rules, the limits that keep the account alive.
Six: routines, what you do before, during and after the session.
The rule: the course writes the framework down so you can learn it, test it against your own record, and keep what holds.

Getting it wrong is treating the course as a promise. This is not a get-rich-quick course. Trading is a skill, and a skill takes time, repetition and honest review. The course cannot tell you whether a setup will pay you. Your record can.

segments.title: Who it is for and how it works

cues.text: Who is this for? Anyone who wants to learn the framework and test it on their own record.

It is written for intraday futures traders, people who open and close trades inside one session. The examples use MNQ, and the framework is written to carry across futures instruments. Your record decides where it holds.
And it suits anyone curious about how day trading actually works, as long as they want a written framework they can test.
Now, how the course works. It is a path, and each module builds on the last.
Modules one to three come first: how to check a claim, the hard rules that keep an account alive, and the mechanics of the instrument, the contract you trade.
Modules four to seven cover why price moves: who is forced to trade, the auction, which is how a market finds its price, what counts as a level, and order flow, the buying and selling at each price.
Modules eight to fifteen are the Blueprint itself. First come the three tiers every trade traces up through: the idea, the setup and the trigger.
An idea is an if-then statement at a named level, written before the session. Idea generation is how you write one.
Then come the setups, the triggers, trade construction and the written plan.
Modules sixteen to twenty are the daily process.
Modules twenty-one to twenty-four are the evidence and the capstone.
The rule: take them in order. Nothing here is alphabetical. Alphabetical would put this welcome fourth from last.
Getting it wrong is jumping to the setups because they look like the interesting part. The lessons on what gives a stop a job come earlier, so you end up placing it by feel.

segments.title: What you need and the philosophy

cues.text: What do you need? Right now, nothing. Just read and learn.
Later, when you are ready to practice, a brokerage account, which is the account your orders go through.
A charting platform. The course uses NinjaTrader 8, with MNQ for its examples.
A trading journal, the record of every trade. Module eighteen covers the habit.
And a pen and paper. Write things down. A pen is the cheapest risk control on the list. It also never needs an update.
One rule before you begin: never risk money you cannot afford to lose.
Trading involves real risk. Risk is covered in Module two and Module fourteen, but this reminder lives here, at the very beginning, on purpose.
Getting it wrong is risking money you need and calling it practice. Once the loss matters to your rent, it starts picking your next move, and the plan stops deciding.
Now, the philosophy. It fits in three lines. One: the setup is the plan.
Two: discipline is the execution.
Three: everything else is noise.

Everything in this course comes back to those lines. Whether a setup holds up for you is a question your own record answers. The course teaches you how to ask it, and shows no trading results of its own.

check.q: What do you need right now to start the course?
check.why: A brokerage account, a charting platform and a journal come later, when you are ready to practice.

check.q: Which platform does the course use for its examples?
options: NinjaTrader 8, with MNQ for its examples
check.why: The examples are illustrated on MNQ.

check.q: What is the one rule before you begin?
options: Never risk money you cannot afford to lose
check.why: Risk is covered in Modules 02 and 14, and the reminder sits at the very beginning on purpose.

check.q: What goes wrong when you risk money you cannot afford to lose?
options: The loss starts picking your next move, and the plan stops deciding
check.why: That is why the rule comes before the first lesson.

cues.text: Everyone reads Modules one to three in order. This check tells you which of them to read slowly.
Answer yes or no to each line, about your trading as it stands now. Be honest. Nobody grades this check except your next trade.
One: you have a daily loss limit, written down and set at your broker, that stops you trading for the day.
Two: you know the hours you are allowed to trade, and the news releases you stay flat for, meaning you hold no position.
Three: you have never moved a stop further away after the trade was on.
Four: you can say, without looking, what one tick and one point of your contract are worth. A tick is the smallest price step. A point is a whole unit of price.
Five: you know which contract month you trade, and the date you have to roll out of it. Rolling means moving to the next contract month before the current one expires.
Six: you can turn a stop distance in points into the money at risk per contract, in your head.
The threshold. Any no on lines one to three means Module two, The Hard Rules, comes before your next trade, live or simulated.
All three yes, but any no on lines four to six, and your gap is the instrument. Work through Module three line by line.
Six of six: read both anyway. The rest of the course assumes every line.
Getting it wrong is answering yes to a line you have never checked. A yes you cannot point to is a no. For each yes, name where it is written down or set.

cues.text: Before your next session, one assignment. Write one line on paper: the most you will lose in one trading day.
Keep it where you trade. That is the whole assignment.
It is one line. It is also the only risk control in the course that fits on a sticky note.
Getting it wrong is keeping the number in your head. A number in your head can move. A number on paper stays where you wrote it.
Summary. Without a written rule and a record, every result is a story.
The course gives you the rules, the vocabulary and the routines to turn your trading into a record you can read.
Where it goes next. Module one, How To Know What You Know, is next: how to check any trading claim, including the ones in this course.
Module two, The Hard Rules, turns your one line into the daily kill switch, the limit that ends your day.
And the journal in Module eighteen, Journaling and Review, is where every trade you take from here on gets recorded against those rules.

check.q: What is the assignment?
options: Write one line on paper: the most you will lose in one trading day, and keep it where you trade
check.why: It is the whole assignment; Module 02 turns the line into a rule.

check.q: Which module turns your one line into the daily kill switch?
check.why: Module 02, The Hard Rules.

check.q: Where does every trade you take from here on get recorded against the rules?
options: The journal in Module 18, Journaling & Review
check.why: The journal is where each trade is recorded.

check.q: Why keep the number on paper where you trade, not in your head?
options: A number in your head can move; a number on paper stays where you wrote it
check.why: The fix is a mechanism, not a mindset: paper, kept where you trade.

questions.q: Which statement is true of the course?
options: It shows trading results of its own
It gives a written framework and the tools to test it on your own record
It promises a setup that pays
questions.why: The course shows no trading results of its own.

questions.q: Complete the philosophy: the setup is the plan, discipline is the execution, and what else?
questions.why: Everything in the course comes back to those three lines.

questions.q: Which modules cover why price moves?
questions.why: Who is forced to trade, the auction, what counts as a level, and order flow.

questions.q: You answer no to line two, the trading hours and news releases. Where do you go?
questions.why: Any no on lines one to three means Module 02 comes before your next trade.

questions.q: What is the one rule before you begin?
options: Never risk money you cannot afford to lose
questions.why: Risk is covered in Modules 02 and 14; the reminder lives at the beginning on purpose.

questions.q: Why write the rule and the stop down before you trade?
options: So a result can be read against the rule, and is not just a story
questions.why: Without a written rule and a record, every result is a story.
